paragraphs: St Bertrand de Comminges is a town fallen into decay on the ridges at the foot of the Pyrenees, not very far from Toulouse and still nearer Bagnères-de-Luchon. It was the seat of a bishop until the Revolution, and its cathedral attracts a certain number of tourists. In the spring of 1883 an Englishman arrived in this old-world place. I can hardly honour it with the name of city, for it has fewer than a thousand inhabitants. He was a Cambridge man who had come especially from Toulouse to see St Bertrand’s Church. He had left two friends at their hotel in Toulouse. They were less enthusiastic archaeologists than he was, and had promised to join him the following morning. Half an hour in the church would satisfy them, and all three could then continue their journey towards Auch. But our Englishman had arrived early that day. He intended to fill a notebook and use several dozen photographic plates while describing and photographing every corner of the wonderful church that dominates the little hill of Comminges. To do this properly, he needed the church’s verger entirely to himself for the day. The rather abrupt woman who keeps the Chapeau Rouge inn therefore sent for the verger, or sacristan. I prefer the latter name, inaccurate though it may be. When he arrived, the Englishman found him an unexpectedly interesting subject for study. It was not the little old man’s thin, shrivelled appearance that interested him: he looked exactly like dozens of other church caretakers in France. It was his strangely furtive air—or rather, his air of being hunted and oppressed. He was constantly half turning to look behind him. His back and shoulders seemed permanently hunched with nervous tension, as though he expected an enemy to seize him at any moment. The Englishman hardly knew what to make of him. Was he haunted by some fixed delusion, weighed down by a guilty conscience, or tormented beyond endurance by a domineering wife? On balance, the last seemed most likely. Yet he gave the impression of having a persecutor more formidable even than a bad-tempered, scolding wife.

However, the Englishman—let us call him Dennistoun—was soon so absorbed in his notebook and so busy with his camera that he could spare the sacristan only an occasional glance. Whenever he looked, the man was close by, either pressing himself back against a wall or crouching in one of the splendid choir stalls. After a while Dennistoun grew rather restless. He began to worry that he was keeping the old man from his meal, or that the man suspected him of planning to steal St Bertrand’s ivory bishop’s staff—or even the dusty stuffed crocodile hanging above the font.
“Won’t you go home?” he said at last. “I’m quite capable of finishing my notes alone. You can lock me in if you like. I’ll need at least another two hours here, and you must be cold, surely?”

“Good heavens!” said the little man. The suggestion seemed to plunge him into an inexplicable terror. “We cannot think of such a thing for a moment. Leave you alone in the church, sir? No, no. Two hours, three hours—it makes no difference to me. I’ve had my breakfast, and I’m not at all cold. Thank you very much, sir.”
“Very well, my little man,” Dennistoun said to himself. “You’ve been warned, and you must take the consequences.”

Before the two hours were up, he had thoroughly examined the choir stalls, the enormous decaying organ, Bishop John de Mauléon’s choir screen, the surviving glass and tapestries, and the objects in the treasury. The sacristan still followed at Dennistoun’s heels. Every now and then he spun round as though something had stung him, whenever he heard one of the strange noises that disturb a large, empty building. Some of those noises were very curious indeed.

“Once,” Dennistoun told me, “I could have sworn I heard a thin, metallic voice laughing high up in the tower. I shot a questioning glance at my sacristan. He was white to the lips. ‘It’s him—that is—it’s no one. The door is locked,’ was all he said. We stared at each other for a full minute.”

Another small incident greatly puzzled Dennistoun. He was examining a large, dark picture hanging behind the altar, one of a series showing St Bertrand’s miracles. It is almost impossible to make out what the picture shows, but the Latin inscription beneath it reads:
How St Bertrand freed a man whom the Devil had long wanted to strangle. (How St Bertrand rescued a man whom the Devil had long tried to strangle.)

Dennistoun was turning to the sacristan with a smile, about to make some joking remark, when he saw something that astonished him. The old man was on his knees, staring at the picture with the look of someone pleading in agony. His hands were tightly clasped, and tears poured down his cheeks. Naturally, Dennistoun pretended not to notice. But he could not stop asking himself, “Why should such a badly painted thing affect anyone so deeply?” He felt he was beginning to find a clue to the strange expression that had puzzled him all day. The man must have some single, overwhelming obsession—but what was it?

It was nearly five o’clock. The short day was ending, and shadows were filling the church. The curious noises—the muffled footsteps and distant voices talking, which had been audible all day—seemed to become more frequent and more insistent. No doubt the fading light had sharpened their hearing.

For the first time, the sacristan showed signs of haste and impatience. He sighed with relief when the camera and notebook were finally packed and put away, and hurriedly beckoned Dennistoun towards the church’s western door, beneath the tower. It was time to ring for the Angelus prayer. A few pulls on the reluctant rope set the great bell Bertrande speaking high above them. She swung her voice up among the pines and down into the valleys, loud with mountain streams. She called the people of those lonely hills to remember and repeat the angel’s greeting to the woman he called Blessed among women. With that, a deep quiet seemed to settle over the little town for the first time that day. Dennistoun and the sacristan left the church.
They began talking on the doorstep.
“You seemed interested in the old choir books in the sacristy, sir.”
“Certainly. I was going to ask whether there was a library in the town.”

“No, sir. Perhaps the cathedral clergy once had one, but it’s such a small place now—” He paused strangely, apparently unable to decide what to do. Then, as if taking a plunge, he continued: “But if you’re a lover of old books, sir, I have something at home that might interest you. It’s less than a hundred yards away.”

All Dennistoun’s treasured dreams of finding priceless manuscripts in unexplored corners of France suddenly blazed up, only to fade again a moment later. It was probably some dull Mass book printed by Plantin around 1580. How likely was it that collectors had not long ago searched every corner of a place so close to Toulouse? Still, it would be foolish not to go. He would reproach himself for ever if he refused. So they set off. On the way, Dennistoun thought again about the sacristan’s strange hesitation and sudden determination. Rather ashamed of himself, he wondered whether he was being lured into some out-of-the-way quarter to be murdered as a supposedly rich Englishman. He therefore managed to start a conversation with his guide. Rather clumsily, he worked in the fact that he expected two friends to join him early the next morning. To his surprise, this news seemed at once to relieve some of the sacristan’s anxiety.
“That’s good,” he said quite cheerfully. “That’s very good. You’ll be travelling with your friends, sir. They’ll always be near you. It’s a good thing to travel with company like that—sometimes.”
The last word seemed to come as an afterthought, and with it the poor little man sank back into gloom.

They soon reached his house. It was built of stone and was rather larger than its neighbours, with a shield carved above the door: the shield of Alberic de Mauléon. Dennistoun tells me that Alberic belonged to a later generation of a side branch of Bishop John de Mauléon’s family. He was a Canon of Comminges from 1680 to 1701. The mansion’s upper windows were boarded up. Like the rest of Comminges, the whole place had the look of old age falling into decay.
On his doorstep, the sacristan paused for a moment.
“Perhaps,” he said, “perhaps, after all, you haven’t the time, sir?”
“Not at all. Plenty of time. Nothing to do until tomorrow. Let’s see what you’ve got.”

At that moment the door opened, and a face looked out. It was much younger than the sacristan’s, but bore something of the same distressing expression. Here, though, it seemed less a fear for personal safety than an intense anxiety for someone else. The young woman was plainly the sacristan’s daughter. Apart from that expression, she was a good-looking girl. She brightened considerably when she saw her father with a strong, healthy stranger. Father and daughter exchanged a few remarks. Dennistoun caught only these words from the sacristan: “He was laughing in the church.” The girl answered them only with a look of terror.

A minute later they were in the sitting room, a small room with a high ceiling and a stone floor. Moving shadows filled it, cast by a wood fire flickering on a large hearth. A tall crucifix on one side, reaching almost to the ceiling, gave the room something of the character of a private chapel. The figure was painted in natural colours; the cross was black. Beneath it stood a solid old chest. Once a lamp had been brought and chairs placed for them, the sacristan went to the chest. With what seemed to Dennistoun growing excitement and nervousness, he took out a large book wrapped in a white cloth. A cross had been roughly embroidered on the cloth in red thread. Even before the covering came off, the book’s size and shape interested Dennistoun. “Too large for a Mass book,” he thought, “and not the shape of a book of church chants. Perhaps it will be something good after all.” A moment later the book lay open, and he felt he had finally found something better than good. It was a large folio volume, perhaps bound late in the seventeenth century, with Canon Alberic de Mauléon’s coat of arms stamped in gold on its covers. There may have been a hundred and fifty paper leaves. Almost every one had a leaf from an illuminated manuscript attached to it. Dennistoun had scarcely imagined such a collection even in his wildest dreams. Here were ten leaves from an illustrated copy of Genesis, certainly no later than A.D. 700. Further on was a complete set of pictures from an English book of Psalms, among the finest the thirteenth century could have produced. Perhaps best of all were twenty leaves of Latin written in rounded capital letters. A few scattered words immediately told him that these must belong to some very early, unknown treatise by one of the Church Fathers. Could this possibly be part of the copy of Papias’s “On the Words of Our Lord” known to have existed at Nîmes as late as the twelfth century? Whatever it was, he had made up his mind. That book must go back to Cambridge with him, even if he had to empty his bank account and remain at St. Bertrand until the money arrived. He glanced up at the sacristan, hoping his face might give some hint that the book was for sale. The man was pale, and his lips were moving.
“If you would turn to the end, sir,” he said.

So Dennistoun turned the pages, finding new treasures with every leaf. At the end he came upon two sheets of paper, much more recent than anything he had seen so far, which puzzled him considerably. They must, he decided, date from the time of the unprincipled Canon Alberic. The Canon had doubtless plundered St Bertrand’s cathedral library to make this priceless scrapbook. The first sheet held a carefully drawn plan of the church’s south aisle and cloisters, instantly recognisable to anyone who knew the place. There were strange signs resembling planetary symbols, and a few Hebrew words in the corners. A cross painted in gold marked the cloister’s north-west corner. Beneath the plan were these lines in Latin:

Answers of 12 December 1694. It was asked: Will I find it? Answer: You will. Will I become rich? You will. Will I live as someone others envy? You will. Will I die in my bed? Yes. (Answers of 12 December 1694. It was asked: Will I find it? Answer: You will. Will I become rich? You will. Will I live as someone others envy? You will. Will I die in my bed? You will.)
“A fine example of a treasure hunter’s record. It quite reminds me of Mr Minor-Canon Quatremain in Old St Paul’s,” Dennistoun remarked, and turned the page.

What he saw next affected him, as he has often told me, more powerfully than he had imagined any drawing or picture could. The drawing itself no longer exists, but I own a photograph of it that fully supports his claim. It was a sepia drawing from the end of the seventeenth century. At first glance, it seemed to show a biblical scene. The setting was an interior, and both the architecture and the figures had that partly classical appearance that artists two hundred years ago thought suitable for pictures of the Bible. On the right sat a king on a throne raised on twelve steps, with a canopy overhead and soldiers on either side. Clearly, this was King Solomon. He leaned forward with his sceptre held out in command. His face showed horror and disgust, but also imperious authority and confidence in his power. The left half of the picture, however, was the strangest. It was plainly the centre of interest. On the stone floor before the throne were four soldiers grouped around a crouching figure, which I must describe in a moment. A fifth soldier lay dead on the floor, his neck twisted and his eyes bulging from his head. The four surrounding guards were looking at the King. The horror in their faces was even greater than his. They seemed prevented from fleeing only by their unquestioning trust in their master. Clearly, all this terror came from the creature crouching among them. I despair of conveying in words the effect that figure has on anyone who looks at it. I remember showing the photograph to a lecturer in the study of living forms—a man of, I was about to say, abnormally sound and unimaginative mind. He absolutely refused to be alone for the rest of that evening. Afterwards he told me that for many nights he had not dared put out his light before going to sleep. Still, I can at least describe the figure’s main features. At first, you saw only a mass of coarse, matted black hair. Then you realised it covered a horrifyingly thin body, almost a skeleton, with muscles standing out like wires. The hands were a dusky, pale colour, covered like the body in long, coarse hairs, and ending in hideous talons. The eyes were picked out in burning yellow, with intensely black pupils, and fixed on the enthroned King with animal hatred. Imagine one of those dreadful bird-catching spiders of South America transformed into a human shape, with an intelligence just below a human being’s. You will have some faint idea of the terror this appalling image inspires. Everyone I have shown the picture to makes the same remark: “It was drawn from life.”

Once the first shock of his overwhelming fright had passed, Dennistoun stole a glance at his hosts. The sacristan had his hands pressed over his eyes. His daughter was looking up at the cross on the wall, feverishly praying with her rosary beads.
At last came the question: “Is this book for sale?”
There was the same hesitation Dennistoun had seen before, followed by the same plunge into determination. Then came the welcome answer: “If you wish, sir.”
“How much are you asking for it?”
“I’ll take two hundred and fifty francs.”
This astonished him. Even a collector’s conscience can sometimes be stirred, and Dennistoun’s was more sensitive than a collector’s.
“My dear man!” he said again and again. “I assure you, your book is worth far more than two hundred and fifty francs. Far more.”
But the reply never changed: “I’ll take two hundred and fifty francs. No more.”

There was really no way to refuse such an opportunity. The money was paid, a receipt signed, and a glass of wine drunk to mark the transaction. Then the sacristan seemed to become a new man. He stood straight. He stopped throwing those suspicious glances over his shoulder. He actually laughed—or tried to. Dennistoun rose to leave.
“May I have the honour of accompanying you to your hotel, sir?” the sacristan asked.
“Oh no, thank you! It’s less than a hundred yards. I know the way perfectly, and the moon is out.”
He pressed the offer three or four times, and Dennistoun refused each time.
“Then you’ll send for me, sir, if—if you need me. Keep to the middle of the road. It’s so rough along the sides.”
“Certainly, certainly,” said Dennistoun, impatient to examine his prize alone. He stepped into the passage with the book under his arm.
There the daughter met him. She seemed eager to do a little business on her own account—perhaps, like Gehazi, to “take something” from the foreigner her father had spared.
“A silver crucifix and a chain to wear round your neck. Perhaps you would be kind enough to accept it, sir?”
Well, really, Dennistoun had little use for such things. What did the young lady want for it?
“Nothing—nothing at all. You’re more than welcome to it, sir.”

She said this, and much more, with such unmistakable sincerity that Dennistoun could only thank her profusely and allow her to put the chain round his neck. It really seemed as though he had done the father and daughter some service they hardly knew how to repay. As he set off with the book, they stood in the doorway watching him. They were still watching when he waved a final goodnight from the steps of the Chapeau Rouge.

Dinner was over, and Dennistoun was shut in his bedroom alone with his purchase. The landlady had shown a special interest in him since he told her he had visited the sacristan and bought an old book from him. He also thought he had heard a hurried conversation between her and the sacristan in the passage outside the dining room. It had ended with something to the effect that “Pierre and Bertrand would be sleeping in the house.”

All this time, a growing uneasiness had been creeping over him. Perhaps it was a nervous reaction after the joy of his discovery. Whatever the cause, he became convinced that someone was behind him, and felt much more comfortable with his back against a wall. Of course, none of this weighed heavily against the obvious value of the collection he had acquired. Now, as I said, he was alone in his bedroom, examining Canon Alberic’s treasures. Every moment revealed something still more delightful.

“Bless Canon Alberic!” said Dennistoun, who had a firmly established habit of talking to himself. “I wonder where he is now. Dear me! I wish that landlady would learn to laugh more cheerfully. She makes one feel as though someone’s lying dead in the house. Another half-pipeful, did you say? Perhaps you’re right. I wonder about that crucifix the young woman insisted on giving me. Last century, I suppose. Yes, probably. Rather a nuisance to wear round the neck—just too heavy. Most likely her father’s been wearing it for years. I think I’ll clean it before I put it away.”

He had taken off the crucifix and laid it on the table when he noticed something resting on the red cloth beside his left elbow. Two or three ideas of what it might be flashed through his mind with the unmeasurable speed of thought.
“A cloth for wiping pens? No, there’s nothing like that in the house. A rat? No, too black. A large spider? I sincerely hope not—no. Good God! A hand like the hand in that picture!”

In another tiny fraction of a second, he had taken it all in. Pale, dusky skin covered nothing but bones and tendons of appalling strength. Coarse black hairs grew longer than any on a human hand. Nails rose from the fingertips and curved sharply downwards and forwards: grey, hard as horn, and wrinkled.

He sprang from his chair with unimaginable, deathly terror clutching his heart. The shape whose left hand rested on the table was rising to its feet behind his chair, its right hand hooked above his scalp. Black, tattered cloth hung about it. The coarse hair covered it just as in the drawing. Its lower jaw was thin—what can I call it?—shallow, like an animal’s. Teeth showed behind black lips. It had no nose. Most horrifying of all were its fiery yellow eyes, with their intensely black pupils, and the triumphant hatred and thirst to destroy life that shone in them. They held an intelligence of a kind: greater than an animal’s, less than a human being’s.

This horror filled Dennistoun with the most intense physical fear and the deepest mental revulsion. What did he do? What could he do? He has never been entirely sure what he said. But he knows he spoke, blindly snatched at the silver crucifix, became aware of the demon moving towards him, and screamed like an animal in hideous pain.

Pierre and Bertrand, the two sturdy little servants who rushed in, saw nothing. But they felt something thrust them aside as it passed out between them, and found Dennistoun unconscious. They stayed up with him that night. His two friends reached St Bertrand by nine the next morning. Although still shaken and nervous, he was almost himself again by then. They believed his story, though only after seeing the drawing and speaking to the sacristan.
At about dawn, the little man had come to the inn on some excuse and listened with the deepest interest as the landlady told him what had happened. He showed no surprise.

“It’s him—it’s him! I’ve seen him myself,” was his only comment. However they questioned him, he gave just one reply: “Twice I’ve seen him; a thousand times I’ve felt him.” He would tell them nothing about where the book had come from, or about his own experiences. “I shall soon sleep, and my rest will be sweet. Why trouble me?” he said.
We shall never know what he or Canon Alberic de Mauléon suffered. Some writing on the back of that fateful drawing may perhaps shed light on the matter:

Solomon’s dispute with a demon of the night. Drawn by Alberic de Mauléon. Versicle: O God, come to my aid. Psalm: He who dwells. Saint Bertrand, who drives demons away, pray for me in my misery. I first saw it on the night of 12 December 1694; soon I shall see it for the last time. I have sinned and suffered, and have more still to suffer. 29 December 1701.

I have never fully understood what Dennistoun thought of the events I have described. Once he quoted a passage from Ecclesiasticus to me: “There are spirits created for vengeance, and in their fury they strike terrible blows.” On another occasion he said, “Isaiah was a very sensible man. Doesn’t he say something about monsters of the night living in Babylon’s ruins? These things are rather beyond our understanding at present.”

Something else he told me struck me, and I understood his feelings. Last year we went to Comminges to see Canon Alberic’s tomb. It is a large marble monument with a carved figure of the Canon in a large wig and a cassock. Beneath it is an elaborate tribute to his learning. I saw Dennistoun speaking for some time with the Vicar of St Bertrand’s. As we drove away, he said, “I hope it isn’t wrong. You know I’m a Presbyterian, but I—I believe there will be ‘Masses said and dirges sung’ for the rest of Alberic de Mauléon’s soul.” Then, with a touch of northern Britain in his voice, he added, “I had no idea they cost so much.”
The book is in the Wentworth Collection at Cambridge. Dennistoun had the drawing photographed, then burnt it on the day he left Comminges after his first visit.
